Supramolecular chemical systems provide access to dynamic assemblies via the aggregative effects of many weak bonding interactions.  Compared to traditional non-covalent interactions, such as hydrogen-bonding, metal coordination, pi-pi stacking, hydrophobic forces, and electrostatic forces, that have been employed to direct molecular self-assembly, much less is known about supramolecular chemistry involving secondary bonding in hypervalent iodine systems.  Hypervalent iodine provides a unique bonding motif and ample opportunities to influence supramolecular order to gain access to new functional materials.  We have a fundamental interest in understanding the reaction scope, kinetics, and reversibility of supramolecular complexes composed of hypervalent iodines.  Realization of these properties and the resulting utilization of these design principles will not only be a significant accomplishment in the rational design of unique supramolecular materials but will also create new classes of matter with non-traditional properties that could have utility for new functional materials.

We delved into the supramolecular chemistry of hypervalent iodine-based macrocycles (HIMs, Figure 1).  These materials are assembled through dynamic secondary-bonding, which is similar to dynamic covalent chemistry. We found that there is not only free interchange of monomers among different macrocycles in solution, but the macrocycles can be reversibly disassembled and reassembled by the addition or removal of anions, respectively (Figure 1A).  HIMs were also capable of forming long range coordination complexes with Li+ and Na+ at the periphery of the macrocycles and not at the center of the oxygen rich core as previously hypothesized (Figure 1B). Pi-extended HIMs that incorporated naphthalene or anthraquinone residues in the macrocycles were also prepared. The enlarged aromatics enabled the co-crystallization of Buckminsterfullerene to form higher order supramolecular complexes (Figure 1C).  More challenging work involved the preparation of cage-like compounds (Figure 1D) and covalent organic frameworks (COF). It was believed that the dynamic secondary bonding lends itself well to the preparation of such materials. We prepared a series of precursor compounds to make these materials but have met obstacles including solubility (cages) and lack of porosity or long range order (COFs).  These synthetic endevours will continue into the future.  Future applications of the materials could include molecular sensors, chiral recognition materials, or dynamic polymer system.

Over the course of this grant, 8 graduate students and 7 undergraduates have been supported in some manner.  Four Ph.D dissertations and one M.S. thesis were completed during this time.  These students have given 3 talks/posters at the national ACS meetings and 4 talks at other research functions specific to this work.  Their careers have had successful trajectories with several taking postdoctoral positions (NYU, UT-Austin, U. Chicago, Clarkson, and Oak Ridge National Lab), industry positions (IBC Materials and Coating Technologies, Inc.), or graduate school positions (U. Illinois, Princeton, Purdue, and SIU).  One undergraduate co-authored four publications and was awarded an NSF GRFP in their senior year at SIU.  The PI created new reaction notecards for Organic Chemistry II that are an extension of his augmented reality work in organic chemistry. The PI took one year of sabbatical leave and worked at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and initiated collaborations on this hypervalent iodine work as well as other projects in carbon capture and hydrogen storage.

This project implements a high-performance research and education network architecture over the existing campus cyberinfrastructure (CI) at Southern Illinois University Carbondale. The project solves the performance bottleneck of the current campus core network and establishes new infrastructures enabling high-throughput data transfer with peer institutions and on-campus private wireless broadband service. The updated CI enables efficient and high-throughput data movement needed by fast-growing data-intensive research and education applications across broad academic domains on campus including Chemistry and Biochemistry, Physics, Engineering, Plant Biology, Statistics, Computer Science, etc. The project builds upon a strong partnership among campus information technology experts, networking faculties, and domain researchers. It also provides an exceptional opportunity to train the CI workforce. 

The project includes three tasks: 1) enhance the campus core network by adding redundancy across 9 core locations with new routers and 10 Gbps links. The updates add the capacity and redundancy needed to offer reliable and high-performance network service to the whole campus; 2) establish a Science DMZ and the associated network performance monitoring framework, which enables researchers to obtain and share data with external hosts a high speed; and 3) establish a private LTE network dedicated to research and education over the 3.65 GHz CBRS spectrum. Five data-intensive science and education applications are prototyped to demonstrate the new CI capabilities and workflows enabled by this project.

The "CC* Networking Infrastructure: Enhancing SIUC Campus Cyberinfrastructure to Accelerate Data-Driven Research and Education" project, funded by the National Science Foundation, was undertaken to address critical limitations within the existing campus cyberinfrastructure at Southern Illinois University Carbondale. This initiative has successfully improved network performance, established a simple Science DMZ for high-speed data sharing, and introduced a private LTE network dedicated to research and education. These advancements have significantly enhanced the capabilities of the university's cyberinfrastructure, allowing for the efficient transfer of high-throughput data vital for the growing demands of data-intensive research and education applications across various academic disciplines.

The project's outcomes include:

1. Enhancement of Campus Core Network

The project has enhanced the campus core network by adding redundancy across nine core locations through the introduction of new routers and 10 Gbps links. This update has substantially increased the network's capacity and redundancy, ensuring the provision of reliable and high-performance network services throughout the entire campus. This enhanced infrastructure has been leveraged to support virtualized learning environments, such as NETLAB+, enabling customized and preconfigured learning content and virtualized systems used in a multitude of ITEC courses.

2. Establishment of a Science DMZ

A Science Demilitarized Zone (Science DMZ) has been established, along with an associated network performance monitoring framework, allowing researchers to efficiently acquire and share data with external hosts at high speeds. This development has proven particularly valuable for the SIU Wabash seismograph site, located approximately two hours from campus, potentially enabling the remote collection of seismic data in the future.

3. Creation of a Private LTE Network

The project has successfully created a private Long-Term Evolution (LTE) network dedicated to research and education, utilizing the 3.65 GHz Citizens Broadband Radio Service (CBRS) spectrum. Two LTE stations have been deployed to support the ongoing campus lake water quality monitoring project. The potential for integration with other LTE deployments on the SIU campus holds promise for broader private LTE coverage, especially for initiatives such as the forest monitoring project.

4. Prototyping Data-Intensive Science and Education Applications

As a culmination of the project, five data-intensive science and education applications have been prototyped, effectively demonstrating the new capabilities and workflows made possible by the enhanced cyberinfrastructure. The project has also supported a total of at least four graduate students and one undergraduate student, providing the necessary resources for hardware, LTE station configurations, and research support in various data-driven science and engineering research endeavors including enviormental engineering, earthquake detection, networking, machine learning etc. 

This NSF-funded project represents a transformative initiative that not only addresses the immediate performance bottlenecks within the existing infrastructure but also lays the foundation for continued growth in data-intensive research and education. Furthermore, it has fostered interdisciplinary collaboration and training opportunities, making it a valuable asset to Southern Illinois University Carbondale.

This award will support a series of three workshops to be held in conjunction with the annual meetings of the Society for the Study of Evolution (19 June 2020, Cleveland, OH), the Botanical Society of American (18 July 2020, Anchorage, AK) and the Ecological Society of America (9 August 2020, Salt Lake City, UT). Without an active effort to disseminate information about Project Baseline, it may not be used to its full potential.
 
These three workshops will include a description of the available resources; examples of recent resurrection studies; the development of guidelines for using seeds; and opportunities for collaborative small-group discussion. Products from the proposed workshops will include: best practices for using and maintaining Project Baseline; literature demonstrating the uses of Project Baseline seeds; a database of potential funding sources for research and future collections; a Project Baseline presentation; and an opportunity to develop a network of research collaborators.

The NSF-funded Project Baseline seedbank has amassed a critical genetic resource to explicitly address questions about temporal and spatial patterns of evolution. The seedbank comprises over 10 million seeds from 65 plant taxa, collected from over 270 sites across the contiguous United States and stored at the National Laboratory for Genetic Resources Preservation. For each taxon, sampling was conducted across multiple populations, with an average of 103 maternal families per population, resulting in over 100,000 maternal lines for experimental studies. The Project Baseline Informational Workshop grant aimed to raise awareness about this valuable collection and availability to researchers across the scientific community, and to stimulate discussions about projects that that could use the Project Baseline seedbank. To achieve these goals, workshops were hosted both virtually and in-person, and significant updates were made to the seedbank databases and webpage. First, a three-part virtual workshop was hosted in Fall 2021, reaching a broad and diverse audience of primarily early career researchers. Over 120 participants registered for the workshops to participate asynchronously or synchronously. A key element of these workshops included example research studies, including a pilot study facilitated by the Project Baseline seedbank. In addition, working luncheons were hosted in conjunction with two conferences in Summer 2022, the Society for the Study of Evolution (Cleveland, OH) and the Botanical Society of America (Anchorage, AK). Over two dozen participants took part in the luncheons, primarily consisting of early career researchers. Researchers spent time networking, forming working groups, and formulating project ideas to use the collections. Importantly, researchers also learned how to use the Project Baseline databases, and how to make requests to access the seed collection. Finally, a portion of this grant was allocated towards updating and maintaining the large databases associated with the collections and making these data available to researchers through the Project Baseline webpage (https://www.baselineseedbank.org/).

The project is to create a new geospatial and hydrological modeling approach that improves the identification of rivers and streams using high-resolution digital elevation models (HRDEMs). Accurate identification of these river and stream networks is necessary for monitoring environmental process such as the transport of nutrients and aquatic species. The results will create an intelligent hydrological model by combining methods in geographic information sciences, artificial intelligence and cyberinfrastructure that will enable multi-scale analysis of river and stream networks. The model, algorithms, and datasets generated from this project will be freely available to the public and benefit a broad scope of natural resources management activities, such as watershed monitoring, wetland conservation, and aquatic species protection. The results of this work will be incorporated into educational curriculums and disseminated to the broader educational community.

There is a critical need for datasets and modeling approaches that can be used to generate hydrologically corrected HRDEMs and delineate hydrologic features like wetlands, road culverts and bridges at a fine scale. To improve the modeling accuracy, this project will develop a geospatial artificial intelligence-hydrological modeling framework that is compatible with HRDEMs. A deep learning model and an image dataset of drainage crossing locations will be developed to identify the locations of hydraulic drainage structures as virtual flow barriers. The effects of hydraulic drainage structures, HRDEM resolutions, and flow direction algorithms on the delineated hydrologic features and their connectivity will be assessed via controlled experiments for an optimal combination. The model will be implemented on high-performance computing clusters to speed up the geocomputation. This project will substantially advance the state-of-the-art of terrain-based hydrologic modeling integrating methods in geographic information science, artificial intelligence, and cyberinfrastructure.

The characterization of hydrologic connectivity is critical for environmental management issues such as overland nutrient loss and fish passage over barriers. The multi-scale delineation of overland flow routing helps understand how hydrologic networks interconnect across agricultural landscapes. However, digital elevation models (DEMs) with high spatial details often exhibit challenges that widespread road bumps block or cause incorrect flow routing at drainage crossing locations. Therefore, a key focus of this project was to develop deep learning approaches to determine the locations of these drainage crossing locations, which is a significant improvement over traditional methods that rely on labor-intensive digitization and field surveys.

One of the key outcomes of this project was the development and application of basic and advanced convolutional neural network (CNN) models for recognizing images containing drainage crossings using high-resolution DEMs and aerial orthophotos. The study finds that CNN models, particularly those utilizing DEMs as the sole input feature, achieve the highest classification accuracy exceeding 93%. The best-fit models exhibit excellent transferability across four watersheds in California, Nebraska, North Dakota, and Illinois respectively. Building on the success of image classification, we developed deep learning models to accurately detect the locations of drainage crossings. Additionally, the research team assessed the effectiveness of processing high-resolution DEMs at these crossing sites to enhance flowline representation. The findings demonstrate that the incorporation of drainage crossings into DEMs significantly improves the precision of flowline delineation, resulting in more accurate representations of drainage features.

The models and datasets developed through this project have been extensively disseminated via peer-reviewed publications, presentations, and NSF-funded training workshops. To date, the project has resulted in ten peer-reviewed articles (including one pending minor revisions) and numerous presentations at national and regional conferences, such as the American Association of Geographers (AAG) annual meetings and the American Geophysical Union (AGU) Fall Meetings. In addition to contributing to the academic community, the project has provided significant training and educational opportunities for researchers at various career stages, including postdoctoral researchers, graduate students, undergraduate students, and even high school students. Notably, one Ph.D. student and one M.S. student, both supervised by the Principal Investigator, completed their dissertation and thesis directly based on this project. Furthermore, the project’s outcomes have supported advanced training in GPU cyberinfrastructure through a separate NSF-funded workshop grant, delivering professional development benefits to approximately 30 graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Finally, the models and datasets developed from this project have been shared with key stakeholders, such as the U.S. Geological Survey, Illinois Departments of Transportation, and academic institutions.

abstractText:
This project aims to serve the national interest by creating safe and inclusive learning environments. Specifically, the project aims to begin a transformation in the way archaeological field school directors implement policies and procedures. Undergraduate education for students who plan to become archaeologists often requires a four- to eight-week field-based learning course, referred to as a field school. Studies have suggested that field-based learning environments can make students susceptible to sexual harassment and related unwelcome behaviors. Undergraduate students who have such experiences may face negative consequences that can derail academic progress, possibly even causing them to leave their chosen field of study or drop out of college. Through this project, the research team will identify and document field school policies, procedures, and structures that promote safe learning environments for undergraduate students pursuing careers in archaeology. The project team will document practical steps that directors of field schools can take to prevent harassment and assault and, by extension, help retain students in the field, ensuring a more diverse workforce in archaeology and other field-based sciences. 

The research team will conduct this work in three phases. Phase 1 will consist of a landscape analysis to document current sexual harassment and assault policies, procedures, and structures that field directors implement. The research team will use the results to select a sample of eight field schools as case studies for Phase 2. Phase 2 will focus on understanding how sexual harassment and assault policies, procedures, and structures are implemented and will gather students' perceptions of safety, and their identity and self-efficacy as an archaeologist in the context of these implementations. The Phase 2 results will allow the project team to identify practices and structures that hold promise for eliminating harassment and assault at field schools. During Phase 3, the research will provide supports to field directors to implement modifications within the sample of case study field schools and evaluate the efficacy of the modified approaches. The final product of this research will be a set of evidence-based practices designed to prevent sexual harassment, assault, and violence at field schools. The research will explore mechanisms field directors can implement to structure learning environments that are free of sexual harassment and assault, helping undergraduate students achieve their full potential to learn. This research will provide foundational data to begin building theory and models to support all undergraduate students to safely engage in field-based research courses. projectOutComesReport:
Evidence-based Transformation of Undergraduate Field Schools to Promote Safety and Inclusivity investigated what archaeological field school directors can do to reduce and prevent sexual harassment at field schools and how students perceive those reduction and prevention practices. Using a mixed-method approach that included surveys and interviews with field school directors and students, the research team developed several recommendations that field directors can implement to support undergraduate student learning at field schools, while also supporting safe and inclusive field learning environments. The team developed seven approaches to support undergraduate student learning at field schools. These include 1) position students as epistemic agents in the field learning process; 2) provide a clear grading structure for students with transparent feedback; 3) support all students to participate in the field school by actively recruiting students and staff who are from backgrounds historically marginalized in STEM, archaeology, and higher education; 4) provide quiet spaces for students and staff; 5) facilitate open communication through daily debriefing meetings to begin and end the day; 6) facilitate open communication between field school leaders and students by encouraging questions; 7) serve as advocates for students and recognize institutionalized barriers that may disempower them.

The team also made nine recommendations that field school directors can implement to reduce sexual harassment at field schools. These include 1) communicate sexual harassment policies clearly, seriously, and in a non-compliance orientated framing; 2) provide readings to students and staff that contextualize the history and impact of sexual harassment on the field of archaeology; 3) connect ethical field behavior with research quality; 4) provide students with the university’s structural mechanisms to report sexual harassment, including the contact information for Title IX administrators, the supervisor of the field school director, anonymous reporting systems, and counseling services; if available, provide contact information for non-university advocacy groups; 5) provide students with contact information of local support structures and/or local advocates if the field school is in a remote location; 6) provide students with an anonymous survey form where they can share issues and concerns they might have with supervisory staff; 7) provide a clear definition of what sexual harassment is and clarify that gender harassment is a form of sexual harassment; 8) provide evidence-based training sessions for supervisory staff, particularly graduate students, that supports their ability to respond to reported cases; and 9) ensure that students are aware of mandatory reporting/responsible employee obligations and who among the field school staff is a mandatory reporter.

This research was widely disseminated by the team, which resulted in a combination of 11 conference presentations and posters, three peer-reviewed publications, and eight workshops to support the adoption of these recommendations among field school directors, staff, and supervising graduate students. As such, this research and the dissemination of the research translates into field-based learning environments that are safer and more inclusive for undergraduate students to learn.
